coverage.assessment: Three revision cuts break causal chains: Europe's waiting is removed from the Bull Run passage, the trouble rotation no longer prepares the aphorism, and the Trent cheer loses its motive. The 'desperate' risk is now asserted without grounds. A first-draft cut also weakened the link between Trent and the end of usefulness.

'No one cared to hurry it' and 'this was all that saved his father' have lost their referent, Europe. Fryston, Mansfield Street and Maurigy's remain clear, and the Minister's absence at Trent is intact.
The chapter has little dialogue. 'amhandheggsir', 'Quel chien de pays!' and 'Surtout point de zele!' survive with their correct speakers and settings.

The revision cut the admission that he never met rudeness, which was the counterweight to the British-prejudice section. Russell's hedge, the 'nearly seven years' forward glance, and the claret/Mill qualification are kept.
Henry's ignorance of Sumner's opposition and the hedged reading of Russell are preserved. Russell is titled 'Lord John' throughout, so there is no anachronism. Nothing later is disclosed early.

The revision trims several cumulative ironic qualifications: the winter gradation and Forster's hidden sentimentality. The father's poise, the martyrs, the leap-frog and the self-correction ('He was mistaken--of course!') keep their timing.
The case that diplomats are indifferent and the secretary useless is thinner, because its premises were cut while its aphorisms were kept. The Sumner-unfitness thread is also weakened.
All four dependencies are intact, with both endpoints present in the actual new drafts.

dependencies.assessment: The Times satire, the grudge and the named Delane survive locally without anticipating 1863. The partner scene in chapter 013 pays this off.

evidence.quote: Mr. Delane lost few opportunities of embittering him
never dreamed of his resentment at being ridiculed in the Times

dependencies.assessment: The pre-arrival recognition and the 'probably intended to act' kindly hedge are kept, and chapter 012 carries the youthful conclusion that Russell lied. Two caveats: the 'understood policy' sentence was cut, and the Russell sentence is still narrator-stated in paragraph 8.

evidence.quote: Lord John Russell had acted--had probably intended to act--kindly by him in forestalling his arrival.
With the insolence of youth and zeal, Henry Adams jumped at once to the conclusion that Earl Russell--like other statesmen--lied

dependencies.assessment: The Lyells remain in the closing list, and chapter 017 echoes the intimacy.

evidence.quote: Sir Charles and Lady Lyell were intimates.
the Lyells were intimate at the Legation

evidence.quote: Monckton Milnes was a social power in London, possibly greater than Londoners themselves quite understood

findings.claim: The revision deleted 'Europe was waiting to see them go.' As a result, 'no one cared to hurry it' now follows the Legation's readiness to leave. 'This was all that saved his father' no longer points to Europe's complacent delay.
findings.counterevidence: A general 'no one' can still be read loosely, but the causal subject is lost.

evidence.quote: Europe was waiting to see them go. So certain was the end that no one cared to hurry it.
Europe was waiting to see them go.
ready to leave England at once, and never assuming more than three months for their limit. So certain was the end that no one cared to hurry it.
So far as a private secretary could see, this was all that saved his father.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the six-word sentence 'Europe was waiting to see them go.' before 'So certain was the end'.
findings.plan_relation: required (Bull Run and the three-month horizon are essential)
findings.reader_effect: The reader cannot tell what saved the Minister. It may even read as if the Legation itself declined to hurry its own end.
findings.title: Europe's waiting cut, leaving 'no one' and 'this' without an antecedent

findings.claim: The revision cut the sentence about quitting a safe seat in Congress with only Sumner's doubtful support. It also cut 'on whom could Seward depend? Certainly not on the Chairman.' The paragraph now jumps from the son's unfitness to 'never before... so desperate'.
findings.counterevidence: The revision's paragraph 4 retains 'Minister Adams had no friend in the Senate', which partly restores the logic later on.

evidence.quote: the weakest of all Mr. Adams's proofs of fitness was his consent to quit a safe seat in Congress for an exceedingly unsafe seat in London
That Mr. Adams was unfit might well be; and no one knew so well as this experienced Senator
Mr. Adams had chosen a private secretary far more unfit than his chief. In the family history, its members had taken many a dangerous risk
No doubt he could depend on Seward, but on whom could Seward depend? Certainly not on the Chairman of the Committee of Foreign Relations.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's 'That Mr. Adams was unfit might well be... likely to give him' sentence, or a short clause about the safe seat and Sumner's support.
findings.plan_relation: required (appointment section; the Minister 'leaving no friend in the Senate')
findings.reader_effect: The climactic judgment seems to rest on the secretary's unfitness rather than on the political exposure. Sumner's role as unhelpful committee chairman also fades.
findings.title: 'So desperate' a family risk now lacks its grounds

findings.claim: The revision cut the reason his solitude was 'doubly desperate', namely that his duties made him escort everywhere. It also cut the Russian/French rotation of troubles, so 'nothing professional in worry' and 'Empires were always tumbling' arrive without the demonstration behind them.
findings.counterevidence: The V6 aphorism survives and remains intelligible in isolation.

evidence.quote: Entire solitude in the great society of London was doubly desperate because his duties as private secretary required him to know everybody
If the American Minister was in trouble to-day, the Russian Ambassador was in trouble yesterday, and the Frenchman would be in trouble to-morrow.
To him, the Legation was social ostracism, terrible beyond anything he had known. In fact he never gave his father the smallest help
No one wanted to discuss affairs. There was nothing professional in worry.

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the first draft's trouble-rotation sentence before 'There was nothing professional in worry'. Also restore the 'doubly desperate... escort' sentence.
findings.reader_effect: The social nightmares lose their mechanism, since he attended those functions as escort. The aphorism becomes a bare assertion instead of a punchline.
findings.title: Absurd position and diplomatic-indifference aphorisms lose their premises

findings.claim: The revision deleted 'They were glad to face the end' and the reasoning that England was waiting to strike, so they were eager to strike first. The shouts of delight are now left unexplained.
findings.counterevidence: 'nervous as wild beasts under the long strain' supplies a partial motive.

evidence.quote: They were glad to face the end. They saw it and cheered it! Since England was waiting only for its own moment to strike, they were eager to strike first.
Since England was waiting only for its own moment to strike, they were eager to strike first.
broke into shouts of delight. They saw it and cheered it!

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the final 'Since England was waiting...' sentence.
findings.plan_relation: required (the Trent news cheered by the secretaries as war; the plan prioritizes the Trent episode)
findings.reader_effect: The paradox of greeting war with joy loses its logic, which follows from the Legation's belief in British hostility. The cheer reads as mere nervous release.
findings.title: Trent cheer loses its stated motive

findings.claim: The first draft cut the explanation that Trent dwarfed individual effort and made zeal too hazardous. That leaves 'Surtout point de zele!' unglossed and the Trent-usefulness link implicit. The revision then also cut the reason no one remembered the satire: others were favorite targets of ridicule.
findings.counterevidence: 'The Trent Affair had one result personal to him' still asserts the link.

evidence.quote: Zeal was too hazardous a profession for a Minister's son to pursue, as a volunteer manipulator, among Trent Affairs and rebel cruisers.
the world had other persons--such as President Lincoln, Secretary Seward, and Commodore Wilkes--for constant and favorite objects of ridicule.

findings.reader_effect: The anecdote reads as a Manchester letter mishap rather than a lesson in proportion amid Trent Affairs. The 'value of obscurity' argument is also thinner.
findings.title: Why the Trent Affair ended 'usefulness' is no longer shown

findings.claim: The revision cut the admission that he could recall no rudeness during that year. It also cut the half-century duration of the Trevelyan friendship.
findings.counterevidence: The revision's paragraph 22 keeps 'Personally the Minister was to be kindly treated'.

He could never recall a single occasion during this trying year, when he had to complain of rudeness.

findings.claim: The revision removed the winter gradation that builds to 'glutton of gloom'. It also removed Forster's 'roughness... to cover' an emotional nature, which was the paradox of his portrait.
findings.counterevidence: The key images survive, and the plan allows condensing the ally portraits.

evidence.quote: Any winter in London is a severe trial; one's first winter is the most trying; but the month of December, 1861
Any winter in London is a severe trial; one's first winter is the most trying
The month of December, 1861, in Mansfield Street, Portland Place, would have gorged a glutton of gloom.
Forster was quite the opposite: a tall, rough, ungainly figure, with no social or political position; pure gold

findings.minimal_repair: Restore the winter gradation clause. Optionally restore the first draft's Forster roughness clause.
findings.reader_effect: The punchlines arrive without their build-up, and Forster is reduced to a contrast with Milnes rather than given his own paradox.
findings.title: Cumulative ironic gradations trimmed

strengths: The father's composure sequence keeps its build: the son's dullness, his unreflecting confidence, then 'not a word escaped; not a nerve twitched'. It is followed by the 'amhandheggsir' release.
The self-correction 'He was mistaken--of course!' and 'nearly seven years longer' remain a forward glance only.
The social nightmares are kept nearly whole, including the leap-frog payoff's deadpan timing.
The Mill anecdote preserves the fine distinction that Henry blamed Mill's assent, not the claret, at the Lodge.
summary: The revision keeps the chapter's spine and all eight verbatim passages. The Delane, Russell, Lyell and Fryston dependencies survive on both ends. Several revision-only cuts remove the premises that later lines depend on. Without 'Europe was waiting to see them go', the claim 'this was all that saved his father' has no clear antecedent. The rotating diplomatic troubles no longer set up the 'Empires' aphorism, the secretaries' Trent cheer loses its stated motive, and the 'desperate' family risk loses its grounds. These are small restorations from the first draft.
